## Summary

CRISPR-Cas systems, base editing, and prime editing have made precise genetic interventions possible, and several approved therapies now treat monogenic disorders that were previously untreatable. Heritable genome editing remains ethically contested. We argue that heritable interventions should not be treated as a single category subject to uniform prohibition. We distinguish three targets: catastrophic monogenic disorders, polygenic risk reduction, and non-disease trait enhancement. For catastrophic monogenic conditions in which preimplantation selection cannot yield unaffected embryos, heritable editing is permissible, and the duty of beneficence toward future persons may require it. When the alternative is certain severe suffering or early death, the expected benefits clearly outweigh the risks. For polygenic interventions, current scientific uncertainty makes clinical application premature: predictive validity remains insufficient and pleiotropic effects are poorly understood. For enhancement, the case is weaker still. Some of its benefits are positional; the risks of social stratification are significant; and the evidence base is absent. We conclude that governance frameworks should permit what the evidence supports under stringent safeguards and prohibit what it does not. The central ethical questions concern welfare, not appeals to nature or abstract notions of dignity. Where the evidence warrants it, failing to pursue heritable gene therapy responsibly may itself be an ethical failure. We outline a translational pathway for ethical germline gene editing.

## Introduction

Cheap, easy, and highly accurate gene-editing platforms have revitalized the field of gene therapy. Once characterized as a “dead end” or a failed enterprise,

Gene therapy is traditionally divided into somatic (modifying specific mature somatic cells) and germline (typically modifying early embryos with modifications passed on to every cell, including germ cells). The idea of treating disease by directly modifying genes was articulated as a theoretical possibility by the 1960s and formalized in early concept papers in the early 1970s.

 These approvals mark the arrival of effective somatic gene therapies, whose effects are confined to the treated individual and are not passed on to future generations.

A further and more ethically challenging prospect is germline gene editing, which involves heritable changes. Germline interventions aim to modify gametes, zygotes, or early embryos so that the resulting genetic changes pass to descendants. Whereas somatic therapies treat individuals already affected by disease, heritable editing aims to prevent disease or otherwise alter traits in future individuals. Moreover, it is much more efficient, potentially modifying every cell in the body. This prospect raises questions about medical safety and about the appropriate boundaries of human intervention in reproduction and evolution.

Debates over the ethics of germline gene editing came to a head in 2018, when the first children with edited genomes were born in China (see Box 1).

 Global condemnation followed, swift and near unanimous. Calls for moratoria and strengthened governance

 reflected a broad recognition that heritable editing in humans remains premature for now. No further gene-edited children have been reported since the 2018 experiment. The underlying controversies persist: some argue that heritable editing should be banned,

 while others hold that it could be permissible under the right circumstances.

Box 1 The 2018 He Jiankui embryo-editing case: technical and ethical failures

In 2018, public reports described the birth of infants following CRISPR-mediated editing of CCR5 in human embryos overseen by He Jiankui. The case failed on several counts. There was no clinical necessity, since existing methods such as prevention of mother-to-child transmission and embryo selection could reduce HIV risk without heritable editing. Preclinical validation was inadequate, with limited assessment of off-target effects and mosaicism. Consent processes were deficient, and oversight was circumvented. For these “illegal medical practices,” He Jiankui received a prison sentence of 3 years.

 The case shows how technical risk, ethical misjudgment, and regulatory gaps can converge, and it points to the need for staged research, stringent review, and transparency.

These rapid developments make it urgent to reexamine the ethical challenges of gene therapy. At the individual level, the central questions concern welfare, risk, and informed consent. At the social level, they turn on fairness, access, and the prospect of new forms of inequality. At the species level, the debate reaches questions of identity, enhancement, and the moral significance of our genetic heritage.

In this review, we assess the ethical implications of advances in gene therapy. The discussion proceeds in three stages. First, it examines the general ethical issues that arise across all forms of gene therapy, including safety, consent, and distributive justice. Second, it considers the specific challenges associated with heritable interventions, such as intergenerational effects, reproductive autonomy, and the reemergence of eugenic concerns. Third, it analyzes distinct categories of therapeutic targets, contrasting interventions aimed at severe monogenic disease, polygenic risk reduction, and non-disease traits. The aim is to identify the principles and institutional mechanisms that can guide the responsible integration of gene therapy into medicine and society.

We adopt a welfare-centric framework throughout: the moral evaluation of a genetic intervention turns primarily on its expected effects on welfare, including the welfare of future persons. Other ethical considerations such as justice and individual autonomy remain relevant, and we note them where they bear on the argument below. Our review of the ethical issues in gene therapy has nonetheless found that welfare considerations carry most of the weight.

## General ethical issues in gene therapy

The ethical issues surrounding gene therapy are in many ways similar to any biomedical innovation. Whether the intervention targets somatic or germline cells, gene therapy raises the same questions: how risks should be weighed against benefits, how consent and comprehension can be secured amid scientific uncertainty and when the intervention affects those unable to decide for themselves, and how the benefits of innovation should be distributed fairly. Because these questions are general to biomedical innovation, the standard approaches to managing and governing it should be fit for purpose for gene therapies as well.

### Safety, risk, proportionality, and precaution

All medical interventions must be justified by a favorable balance of expected benefits over harms. Gene therapy, by intervening at the molecular substrate of heredity, raises challenges in evaluating this balance.
